Clinical Vignette: Margaret

Margaret sits in the consultation room with her hands folded tightly in her lap, her shoulders drawn up toward her ears. At forty-six, she carries herself with the careful precision of someone accustomed to control—a habit developed over two decades working as a veterinarian. But something has shifted in her bearing since she returned from Aleppo eighteen months ago.

She had gone as a volunteer with an international animal welfare organization, driven by the same compassion that drew her to veterinary medicine in the first place. For the first three weeks, the work felt purposeful despite the deteriorating conditions. She treated injured donkeys, cats displaced from destroyed homes, dogs suffering from malnutrition. The clinic operated in a basement, and she learned to work by candlelight when the generators failed. Margaret tells this part of the story methodically, as though reciting facts from a medical journal.

Then the building next to the clinic was hit during an airstrike. She was treating a shepherd's dog when the blast wave knocked her backward into the concrete wall. The dog survived. Two of her colleagues did not. For several seconds afterward, she remembers only ringing silence and the taste of dust. Then the screaming started—human and animal voices blending together in a chaos she couldn't parse or control.

She was evacuated three days later. Her husband, David, says she seemed relatively composed when she returned home to Melbourne. She debriefed with the organization, attended a counseling session, and returned to her veterinary practice. For the first few months, she functioned. She saw patients, completed her rounds, came home to their quiet house in the suburbs.

But the baseline has shifted. Margaret now startles violently at unexpected sounds—the microwave beeping, a car backfiring, even David touching her shoulder from behind. Her sleep is fractured and haunted. She wakes at three or four in the morning, her heart hammering, drenched in sweat, often unable to remember what she was dreaming about. The exhaustion accumulates like sediment.

At work, she finds herself unable to focus during routine procedures. Last month, while examining a cat with a respiratory infection, she became convinced the animal was suffocating. Her hands began to shake. She had to excuse herself and sit in her office for twenty minutes, breathing deliberately, before she could return to complete the examination. She's always been the calm one, the steady presence in the clinic. Now her staff notices her irritability, the way she snaps at minor mistakes.

Margaret avoids anything that reminds her of that day. She no longer watches news coverage of Syria or any conflict zone. She's declined three invitations to social gatherings because she knows there will be crowds and unpredictable noise. David wants to take her to his company dinner next month, but the thought of sitting in a crowded restaurant, unable to see exits clearly, unable to control her environment, fills her with dread.

The hypervigilance is exhausting. She finds herself scanning rooms for danger, noting exits, assessing threats that rationally she knows aren't present. In the supermarket last week, she felt trapped by the fluorescent lights and the press of other shoppers. She abandoned her cart and left.

What troubles her most is the guilt. The shepherd's dog lived. Her colleagues didn't. She was trained to save lives; in Aleppo, she couldn't save the ones that mattered most. She tells David she should be fine, that she's stronger than this, that she's seen worse things in her career. But the truth is, she's not fine. She's stuck in that basement, waiting for the next blast.
